title.text: When Does Image Generation Help Image Understanding?

source.raw_tex: \title{When Does Image Generation Help Image Understanding?}

description.text: Image generation provides dense supervision over visual structure, yet prior work has found surprisingly limited transfer from generation data to visual understanding.

source.raw_tex: Image generation provides dense supervision over visual structure, yet prior work has found surprisingly limited transfer from generation data to visual understanding.

abstract_open.text: Image generation provides dense supervision over visual structure, yet prior work has found surprisingly limited transfer from generation data to visual understanding. We revisit this asymmetry by studying training-time transfer from image generation to visual understanding. Using controlled pairs of image-to-image (I2I) and image-to-text (I2T) tasks that share the same input and underlying visual operation, we find that I2I supervision can substantially improve I2T understanding under an appropriate training recipe, with gains increasing as more I2I data is added.

source.raw_tex:
Image generation provides dense supervision over visual structure, yet prior work has found surprisingly limited transfer from generation data to visual understanding.
We revisit this asymmetry by studying training-time transfer from image generation to visual understanding.
Using controlled pairs of image-to-image (I2I) and image-to-text (I2T) tasks that share the same input and underlying visual operation, we find that I2I supervision can substantially improve I2T understanding under an appropriate training recipe, with gains increasing as more I2I data is added.

abstract_map.text: To characterize transfer beyond matched task pairs, we introduce UniTaskonomy, a unified capability taxonomy for generation and understanding, and use it to construct a capability-level transfer map that reveals which kinds of generation data benefit which understanding capabilities. The map reveals highly task-dependent transfer: some gains follow intuitive capability correspondences, while others emerge across different capabilities, and the same generation task can help some targets while interfering with others.

source.raw_tex:
To characterize transfer beyond matched task pairs, we introduce \methodname, a unified capability taxonomy for generation and understanding, and use it to construct a capability-level transfer map that reveals which kinds of generation data benefit which understanding capabilities.
The map reveals highly task-dependent transfer: some gains follow intuitive capability correspondences, while others emerge across different capabilities, and the same generation task can help some targets while interfering with others.

abstract_alignment.text: Finally, in our controlled setting, we found stronger transfer is associated with greater gradient alignment between generation and understanding objectives, particularly in normalization parameters. Taken together, our results challenge the view that generation provides little value for understanding: generation can provide effective supervision for visual understanding, but whether it transfers depends critically on how it is trained and what visual capability it supervises.

source.raw_tex:
Finally, in our controlled setting, we found stronger transfer is associated with greater gradient alignment between generation and understanding objectives, particularly in normalization parameters.
Taken together, our results challenge the view that generation provides little value for understanding: 
generation can provide effective supervision for visual understanding, but whether it transfers depends critically on how it is trained and what visual capability it supervises.

overview_caption.text: When does generation help understanding? (a) Increasing I2I supervision can steadily improve downstream I2T performance, while the effect depends strongly on the training recipe. (b) Across visual capabilities, transfer is highly task-dependent: some I2I–I2T pairs yield large gains, whereas others interfere with understanding (blue/red denote positive/negative transfer; bubble size denotes magnitude). (c) This selectivity is also reflected inside the model, where gradient alignment between I2I and I2T objectives varies sharply across parameter groups and is strongest in pre-attention normalization. Together, these observations motivate our study of when, where, and why generation helps understanding.

source.raw_tex:
\textbf{When does generation help understanding?}
(a) Increasing I2I supervision can steadily improve downstream I2T performance, while the effect depends strongly on the training recipe.
(b) Across visual capabilities, transfer is highly task-dependent: some I2I--I2T pairs yield large gains, whereas others interfere with understanding (blue/red denote positive/negative transfer; bubble size denotes magnitude).
(c) This selectivity is also reflected inside the model, where gradient alignment between I2I and I2T objectives varies sharply across parameter groups and is strongest in pre-attention normalization.
Together, these observations motivate our study of \emph{when, where, and why} generation helps understanding.

controlled_heading.text: Does image generation help visual understanding?

source.raw_tex: \section{Does image generation help visual understanding?}

controlled_setup.text: We first study whether image generation can improve visual understanding at all. Studying this requires a clean setting to test whether knowledge learned from generation tasks can transfer to understanding tasks. We therefore construct controlled tasks in which the generation and understanding objectives require solving essentially the same visual task, differing primarily in the required output modality. This allows us to examine whether the generation objective itself provides useful supervision for visual understanding.

recipe_heading.text: How Should Generation and Understanding Be Combined?

source.raw_tex: \subsection{How Should Generation and Understanding Be Combined?}

recipe_setup.text: We next study how I2I and I2T supervision should be combined during training. We compare an I2T-only baseline (R1) with five training recipes: (R2) I2I pretraining followed by I2T finetuning, with the shared understanding weights updated during I2I training; (R3) mixed I2I-I2T training followed by I2T finetuning; (R4) I2I pretraining with the understanding weights frozen, followed by mixed training; (R5) mixed training throughout; and (R6) I2I pretraining with the understanding weights updated, followed by mixed training.

recipe_result.text: We therefore use I2I pretraining followed by I2T finetuning as the default recipe in subsequent experiments.

taxonomy_heading.text: UniTaskonomy: A Unified Taxonomy of Visual Capabilities

source.raw_tex: \section{\methodname: A Unified Taxonomy of Visual Capabilities}

taxonomy_intro.text: Existing benchmarks organize visual tasks primarily by task formulation or output modality, resulting in largely separate taxonomies for understanding and generation. This makes it difficult to determine how seemingly different tasks relate in terms of the visual information they require. We introduce UniTaskonomy, a shared hierarchy that organizes I2I supervision objectives and I2T evaluation capabilities according to the visual information they target, rather than their output modality.

We introduce \methodname, a shared hierarchy that organizes I2I supervision objectives and I2T evaluation capabilities according to the visual information they target, rather than their output modality.

taxonomy_count.text: The resulting taxonomy contains 15 I2I supervision leaves and 25 I2T capability leaves, with leaf type explicitly indicating whether a node represents a training objective or an evaluation capability. This yields a common visual hierarchy in which generative and understanding tasks can be compared directly without asserting task equivalence.

taxonomy_caption.text: UniTaskonomy. A unified taxonomy of visual tasks organized into three broad families: Recognition, Reconstruction, and Reorganization. Each leaf is explicitly typed as either an I2I supervision objective or an I2T evaluation capability, allowing the two modalities to share the same visual hierarchy without conflating their task identities.

source.raw_tex:
\textbf{UniTaskonomy.}
A unified taxonomy of visual tasks organized into three broad families: \textit{Recognition}, \textit{Reconstruction}, and \textit{Reorganization}. Each leaf is explicitly typed as either an I2I supervision objective or an I2T evaluation capability, allowing the two modalities to share the same visual hierarchy without conflating their task identities.

taxonomy_annotation.text: Once the capability vocabulary is finalized, we separately assign each I2T benchmark sample to its primary capability leaf. To scale this annotation, three independent LLM judges label each sample according to the finalized taxonomy and annotation guidelines, and the final label is determined by majority vote. A sample is retained when at least two of the three judges agree on its label, and samples without a two-of-three consensus are excluded.

source.raw_tex: \section{Which image-editing tasks help which visual capabilities?}

transfer_intro.text: The controlled experiments above show that image-editing supervision can improve image understanding. We now ask: which types of generation data help which visual capabilities? Using UniTaskonomy, we construct a comprehensive generation-to-understanding transfer map that relates individual I2I supervision tasks to downstream I2T capabilities.

related_heading.text: I2I supervision improves related visual capabilities.

source.raw_tex: \paragraph{I2I supervision improves related visual capabilities.}

related_results.text: Several I2I tasks yield gains on understanding capabilities that require closely related visual information. The clearest example is Object pointing: training the model to mark every instance matching a category query produces the largest observed improvement on Counting (+3.57 pp). Here, the image-valued supervision explicitly requires identifying individual instances, a visual requirement shared with counting. Similarly, Z-depth produces the largest gain on Metric 3D relation (+2.90 pp), connecting depth prediction to metric spatial reasoning. 2.5D segmentation also substantially improves 2D Ordering (+11.58 pp). These results show that supervision provided through image targets can improve performance on related visual questions.

source.raw_tex:
Several I2I tasks yield gains on understanding capabilities that require closely related visual information.
The clearest example is \textit{Object pointing}: training the model to mark every instance matching a category query produces the largest observed improvement on \textit{Counting} ($+3.57$ pp).
Here, the image-valued supervision explicitly requires identifying individual instances, a visual requirement shared with counting.
Similarly, \textit{Z-depth} produces the largest gain on \textit{Metric 3D relation} ($+2.90$ pp), connecting depth prediction to metric spatial reasoning.
\textit{2.5D segmentation} also substantially improves \textit{2D Ordering} ($+11.58$ pp).
These results show that supervision provided through image targets can improve performance on related visual questions.

cross_heading.text: Gains also extend across capability families.

source.raw_tex: \paragraph{Gains also extend across capability families.}

cross_results.text: Useful transfer is not limited to these direct correspondences. Colorization yields the largest observed gain on Visual correspondence (+5.71 pp), while 2D keypoints performs best on Multi-view reasoning (+7.38 pp). These pairs cross the Reconstruction–Reorganization boundary in UniTaskonomy, showing that beneficial supervision can also come from tasks outside the target capability's family.

Useful transfer is not limited to these direct correspondences.
\textit{Colorization} yields the largest observed gain on \textit{Visual correspondence} ($+5.71$ pp), while \textit{2D keypoints} performs best on \textit{Multi-view reasoning} ($+7.38$ pp).
These pairs cross the Reconstruction--Reorganization boundary in \methodname, showing that beneficial supervision can also come from tasks outside the target capability's family.
